title: Economic Outlook and the Labor Market
summary: Vice Chair Philip Jefferson presented his economic outlook on April 7, 2026, characterizing the economy as growing in line with potential (approximately 2% GDP growth), with the labor market roughly in balance at 4.3% unemployment and inflation remaining above the Fed's 2% target at approximately 2.8% PCE headline and 3.0% core. Jefferson noted that progress on disinflation has stalled over the past year due to tariffs, and elevated energy prices will apply near-term upward pressure on inflation, while trade policy uncertainty and geopolitical tensions pose upside risks to his forecast.
key_points: PCE price index rose 2.8% for 12 months ending February; core PCE (excluding food and energy) rose 3.0% over the same period
Unemployment rate edged lower to 4.3% in March 2026, near estimated natural rate and down from 4.5% peak in November 2025
March payrolls added 178,000 jobs; Q1 2026 average approximately 70,000 jobs per month, described as somewhat subdued but within breakeven range for steady unemployment
Labor market characterized as 'low-hire, low-fire' with firms pausing workforce expansion rather than conducting widespread layoffs
Core goods inflation increased while housing services declined, with core services ex-housing moving sideways—offsetting factors stalled overall disinflation progress
Trade policy uncertainty, tariffs, Middle East conflict, and elevated energy prices cited as upside risks to inflation forecast
why_it_matters: Vice Chair Jefferson's speech provides a detailed personal assessment from a senior FOMC voter on the inflation-labor market tradeoff. His characterization of stalled disinflation progress, combined with near-term energy price pressures and tariff-related uncertainty, suggests the Fed will need compelling evidence of resumed disinflation before cutting rates. Markets tracking the rate path should monitor whether the 'low-hire, low-fire' labor market dynamic persists, as it implies limited firing pressure even as hiring slows.
macro_context: Jefferson presents a balanced outlook with risks on both sides of the dual mandate—elevated and sticky inflation alongside a labor market near full employment. The Fed's expectation appears to be that disinflation resumes once tariff effects fade, but near-term energy price pressures complicate the timeline. High uncertainty surrounds the outlook due to trade policy uncertainty, geopolitical tensions, and unknown duration of Middle East disruptions.
important_numbers: 2.8% — PCE headline inflation (12 months ending February 2026)
3.0% — PCE core inflation (12 months ending February 2026)
